---
title: "Tutorials"
---

The tutorials combine explanation, maintained Python and C++ source code, and
output produced by pySEB during the documentation build.

Follow the numbered learning path below, or jump to the stage that matches
your experience. Within each stage, tutorials appear in a suggested order.
The focused sequences name required reading in **Before you start** notes. Read
those pages first if the listed concepts are new to you. Continuation pages
include setup for a fresh kernel; you do not need to keep an earlier notebook
running. For installation, visualization controls, and troubleshooting, see
[Using pySEB](../using-pyseb.qmd). For model assumptions and intensity
conventions, see [Theory](../theory.qmd).

## 1. Start here

**Before starting:** No prior pySEB experience is required. Follow these four
tutorials in order:

| Step | Tutorial | What you will learn |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [Introduction to pySEB](introduction.qmd) | Understand scattering, subunits, reference points, structure graphs, parameters, and q |
| 2 | [Your first scattering model](first-model.qmd) | Install pySEB, evaluate a solid sphere, make a plot, and change its radius |
| 3 | [What is a reference point?](reference-points.qmd) | Distinguish scattering material from attachment locations, including fixed and distributed references |
| 4 | [Your first composite model](diblock-copolymer.qmd) | Connect two Gaussian polymers and use the same structure from Python and C++ |

## 2. Build larger structures

**Before starting:** Complete Your first composite model, or be comfortable
adding subunits, linking reference points, and supplying model parameters.

| Tutorial | What you will learn |
| --- | --- |
| [Rod–coil copolymer](rod-coil.qmd) | Compare rigid and flexible blocks at matched overall size, then change contrast |
| [Comb polymer](comb-polymer.qmd) | Compare branched and linear connectivity at fixed composition |
| [Sphere–polymer micelle](micelle.qmd) | Attach tagged chains to distributed sphere-surface references |
| [Random-walk rod chain](random-walk-rods.qmd) | Link rigid segments, calculate the chain size, and compare with a Gaussian polymer |
| [Reuse a composite component](nested-structures.qmd) | Instantiate a diblock twice and share its parameters |
| [Assemble multiple hierarchy levels](nested-hierarchy.qmd) | Reuse a component inside a larger structure and address deeper paths |
| [Parameter sweeps](parameter-sweeps.qmd) | Reuse one graph with several parameter sets |

## 3. Understand the calculations

**Before starting:** Complete Your first scattering model and
[What is a reference point?](reference-points.qmd). Start with the
point-cloud example to calculate the three factors from coordinates, or the
distance-vector derivation to derive an analytical subunit. Composite models
and basic symbolic algebra are useful for the expression-export page.

| Tutorial | What you will learn |
| --- | --- |
| [Scattering from a point cloud](scattering-quantities.qmd) | Build a weighted point cloud and get F, A, and Ψ from point-pair and reference distances |
| [Derive a subunit from distance vectors](scattering-from-phases.qmd) | Derive a rod: form factor, midpoint amplitude, shifted-reference amplitudes, and phase factors; validate a usable subunit |
| [Symbolic expressions and export](symbolic-expressions.qmd) | Select a backend, inspect expressions, convert to SymPy, and export Python, LaTeX, and C forms |

**Before starting:** Be comfortable building composite structures and evaluating

| [Add a reference to an existing subunit](add-subunit-reference.qmd) | Derive two symmetric rod references, extend their YAML definition, and attach polymers there |
| [Save, reload, and visualize a model](save-load-model.qmd) | Preserve topology, verify a round trip, and export a realization |
| [PDB cloud with an attached polymer](pdb-polymer.qmd) | Combine coordinate-based numerical scattering with an analytic subunit |
| [Evaluate mixed models](mixed-model-evaluation.qmd) | Evaluate structures containing numerical, integrated, and analytic subunits with one API |

## 5. Fit experimental data

**Before starting:** Be comfortable building models and exploring parameter
sets. Basic familiarity with least-squares fitting is useful. Follow each
application’s pages in order. For coordinate-based titin domains,
first work through PDB cloud with an attached polymer.

| Tutorial | What you will learn |
| --- | --- |
| [Fit real contrast-variation SANS data](fit-real-sans-data.qmd) | Fit a linked sphere-and-shell structure simultaneously to three experimental datasets |
| [Build a polymer corona](fit-f127-corona.qmd) | Reuse a segmented arm and attach copies to a core |
| [Fit the corona to F127 data](fit-f127-data.qmd) | Define residuals, optimize dimensions, and inspect the fitted model |
| [Compare corona models](compare-f127-coronas.qmd) | Compare alternative arm descriptions using the same data |
| [Fit analytic domains and a linker](fit-linked-titin.qmd) | Fit a titin doublet and diagnose an implausibly small linker |
| [Connect coordinate domains](titin-coordinate-domains.qmd) | Replace adjustable domain shapes with fixed PDB coordinates |
| [Test atomic scattering and hydration](titin-hydration.qmd) | Compare atomic and solvent assumptions with held-point checks |
| [Test relative scattering weights](titin-relative-weights.qmd) | Diagnose the domain-to-chain amplitude ratio |

## Reference and alternative formats

These extended guides offer broader coverage and a C++ route through the
examples. They are optional references alongside the learning path.

The focused sequences use Python. Maintained C++ versions of the original
examples remain in the task pages and the C++ guide below; their listings are
compiled and their output is captured during the build. The complete nested
example appears in [Assemble multiple hierarchy levels](nested-hierarchy.qmd).
The YAML sequence's save/load page also includes portable C++ file APIs.

[Symbolic and numerical scattering with Python](pyseb_tutorial.qmd) covers:

- analytic Gaussian-polymer structures;
- symbolic expressions and vector q evaluation;
- finite-sphere Debye clouds;
- callback-defined numerical subunits;
- PDB parsing and atom parameter profiles;
- mixed numerical and analytic structures.

[C++ modelling tutorials](cpp_tutorials.qmd) compile and run seven C++14
programs:

1. a Gaussian diblock copolymer;
2. a sphere–polymer micelle;
3. reusable nested structures;
4. a random-walk chain of thin rods;
5. a parameter sweep written as CSV;
6. a PDB-derived Debye cloud with an attached polymer;
7. structure inspection and hierarchy diagnostics.

The displayed C++ is included directly from the compiled source files. The
terminal output beneath each program is captured from the executable during
the Quarto render.
